section.title: Simpson’s Rule
section.p: The midpoint and trapezoidal rules replaced the graph by something simple: a horizontal line or a straight line. Those approximations are easy to compute, and their errors are controlled by curvature.
But a curve is not usually straight. On a short interval, a better first picture may be a parabola.
That is the idea behind Simpson’s Rule.
section.md: \text{Use a quadratic curve instead of a line.}
section.p: The reward is surprisingly large. Midpoint and trapezoidal errors usually shrink like 1/n^2. Simpson’s Rule, for smooth functions, usually shrinks like 1/n^4.

exercise.title: Why does Simpson’s Rule use three sample points at a time?

statement.p: A line is determined by two points, while a parabola is determined by three. In your own words, why does Simpson’s Rule therefore work on pairs of subintervals, and why must composite Simpson’s Rule use an even number of subintervals?

hint.p: Three equally spaced values determine one quadratic interpolant. Pairing subintervals means n is even.

statement.p: So Simpson’s Rule is exact in this example.
That should not be surprising. Simpson’s Rule integrates the quadratic interpolating polynomial. If the original function is already quadratic, the approximation is the function itself.

paragraphs.title: Warning: n must be even
paragraphs.p: Composite Simpson’s Rule pairs neighboring subintervals. If n is odd, one subinterval is left unpaired.

For example, n=5 gives five subintervals. Simpson’s Rule can cover four of them in two pairs, but one remains. In that situation, either change n to an even number or combine Simpson’s Rule with another rule on the leftover interval.
For this course, when using Simpson’s Rule, choose n even.

exercise.title: What fails when the fourth derivative is unbounded?

statement.p: Simpson’s Rule can still be applied to \int_0^1\sqrt{x}\,dx, even though f^{(4)} blows up at x=0. In your own words, what exactly fails in that situation, and what does that teach about trusting a formula that still returns a number?

hint.p: The numerical rule can still be used. The theorem that estimates its error is what no longer applies.

Since both integration and Simpson’s formula are linear, exactness for these four powers gives exactness for every cubic.

note.title: Key fact
note.p: Simpson’s Rule is built from a quadratic approximation, but it integrates every cubic polynomial exactly.

subsection.p: This is why Simpson’s Rule can outperform what its construction suggests.

There is also a useful geometric way to remember the improvement. On a concave-up graph, the trapezoidal rule tends to overestimate and the midpoint rule tends to underestimate. Simpson’s Rule is the weighted average
on a single interval, where T is the one-trapezoid approximation and M is the midpoint approximation.
The leading curvature errors of T and M have opposite signs. Simpson’s Rule combines them in just the right proportion to cancel much of that error.

exercise.title: Why is Simpson’s Rule exact for cubics, not only quadratics?

statement.p: Simpson’s Rule is built by integrating a quadratic interpolant, yet it also integrates every cubic exactly. In your own words, why is that possible, and how does writing Simpson as the weighted average \frac13 T+\frac23 M help explain the improvement?

hint.p: On a symmetric interval, the odd cubic term integrates to zero in both the true integral and Simpson’s formula. The leading curvature errors of the trapezoid and midpoint have opposite signs.

subsection.p: The midpoint and trapezoidal error bounds were controlled by f”, because lines fail when curvature is present.
Simpson’s Rule is exact for cubics. So its first possible error comes from behavior beyond cubic. That is why the fourth derivative appears.

note.title: A bound is a guarantee, not a prediction
note.p: An error bound tells us the approximation cannot be worse than a certain amount. It does not usually tell us the actual error exactly.

paragraphs.title: Why the hypotheses matter
paragraphs.p: The Simpson error bound assumes that f^{(4)} exists, is continuous, and is bounded on the interval.
For example,

exists. But the derivatives of f become singular near x=0. In particular, the fourth derivative is unbounded near 0.
Simpson’s Rule may still produce useful approximations, but the standard Simpson error bound does not apply on [0,1].
paragraphs.md: \text{The numerical rule can still be used. The guarantee is what fails.}
paragraphs.p: That warning is important in computation. A formula can return a number even when the theorem that estimates its error does not apply.
Numerical integration approximates accumulation. But the other half of calculus can also be approximated. If we know values of a function from data, can we estimate its derivative?
That question leads to numerical differentiation.
